title: Reading wisdom: Proverbs and Job

objectives.can: Read two-line proverbs and a passage of Job, coping with rare words by their parallel.

explanation.summary: Proverbs packs a saying into two lines, most often with a contrast between the wise and the foolish or the righteous and the wicked. Job is harder: it has rare words and compressed lines. Both are read the same way, by finding the lines, finding what answers what, and letting the partner line help with a word you do not know, as a guide and not as a proof.

sections.heading: The two-line saying
body: The sayings of Proverbs 10 are one verse long and two lines long. Their heading, in 10:1, is מִשְׁלֵי שְׁלֹמֹה, 'proverbs of Solomon'. A saying of this kind states what is commonly seen, in a form that is easy to remember. Scholars generally read such sayings as general observations about how life tends to go. They are not promises, and they are not laws for every case.

The usual shape is antithetic. The first line states one side, the second the other, with the conjunction ו at the start of the second line meaning 'but'. The wise son is set against the foolish son in 10:1, and the righteous against the wicked in 10:6, 10:7 and 10:11. Look for the pairs of opposites: חָכָם and כְּסִיל, צַדִּיק and רְשָׁעִים, שִׂנְאָה and אַהֲבָה.

head: Verse
Line one
Line two
The contrast
rows: gathers in summer, sleeps in harvest
the memory of the righteous, the name of the wicked
hatred stirs up strife, love covers wrongs

sections.heading: Verbless lines and participles
body: Proverbs uses clauses with no verb and clauses with a participle as the subject. In 10:1 the second line, וּבֵן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ, has no verb: 'and a foolish son (is) the grief of his mother'. It is a nominal clause of the kind you met earlier, and the verb of the first line is not carried over.

A participle can be 'the one who does'. In 10:5, אֹגֵר בַּקַּיִץ is 'the one who gathers in summer', and it is the subject of a nominal clause: it is a wise son. In 10:9 הוֹלֵךְ בַּתֹּם, 'the one who walks in integrity', is the subject of the yiqtol יֵלֶךְ. Yiqtol verbs in sayings often state what regularly happens, and the time is not past or future in particular.

sections.heading: Job: rare words and compressed lines
body: Job is a long poem in dialogue and is often very beautiful and very hard. It has rare vocabulary: a good number of words occur once or twice in the whole Hebrew Bible. A word that occurs once is called a hapax legomenon, 'said once'. The lines are also compressed, with words left out and questions packed into a few words.

Many passages read without difficulty. In 28:12, וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא, 'and wisdom, from where is it found?', is a plain question, and the second line is a parallel question: וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם בִּינָה, 'and where is the place of understanding?'. The same question recurs in 28:20, and a repeated line like this is a refrain that marks the turning points of the poem.
Short clauses with no verb occur too: in 28:14, תְּהוֹם אָמַר לֹא בִי הִיא, 'the deep says: not in me is it', the word הִיא is wisdom, a feminine noun, and the clause means 'it is not in me'.

sections.heading: The parallel line as a guide to a rare word
body: When a word is rare, look at the partner line. Job 28:15 says לֹא יֻתַּן סְגוֹר תַּחְתֶּיהָ וְלֹא יִשָּׁקֵל כֶּסֶף מְחִירָהּ. The word סְגוֹר is unusual: the library holds it twice, here and in Hosea 13:8, where it has a different sense. In Job, the second line has כֶּסֶף, 'silver', weighed out as a price, so סְגוֹר stands in the place of something that is given in exchange and ranks with silver. Most readers take it as a precious metal or valuable.

In Job 38:5 the word מְמַדֶּיהָ occurs nowhere else in the analysed text. It stands in a question about the founding of the earth, and the second line has נָטָה עָלֶיהָ קָו, 'stretched a measuring line over it'. The line points to a sense like 'its measurements'.

These are guides and not proofs. A partner line tells you what kind of thing a word is, not its exact meaning, and the same word can mean something else in another place. Lexicons, ancient translations and related languages are all used, and where they disagree the dictionary entries often say that the sense is uncertain. Hold such a reading lightly.

sections.heading: A way to read a verse of wisdom
body: First find the lines, using the sense and the pairs of lines. Second, find the pairs: what answers what? Third, check for a left-out verb. Fourth, for a participle ask whether it is 'the one who'. Fifth, for a rare word look at the partner line and the verse around it, and say what you are sure of and what you are not.

misunderstandings: A proverb is not a promise or a law. It states what is commonly seen, and the book of Job itself shows that life can run another way.
A rare word's meaning cannot simply be read off its parallel. The parallel tells you the kind of thing, and other evidence has to settle the rest.
A participle is not always 'is doing'. In sayings it is very often 'the one who does', the subject of the line.
Job is not unreadable. Most of its lines are clear, and the difficulties are in particular words and a few places where translators differ.

deeper.heading: Hapax legomena and how scholars handle them
body: A word that occurs once cannot be checked against another use in Hebrew. Scholars compare cognate languages such as Aramaic, Arabic and Akkadian, the ancient translations, and the Jewish commentators. Each method has limits: a cognate may have drifted in meaning, and an ancient translator may have guessed. A careful reader keeps track of which evidence supports a given gloss.
The count of a word depends on the text and on how its forms are grouped under headwords. The figures in this lesson are the counts of the analysed library text.

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father; but a foolish son is the grief of his mother.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The heading מִשְׁלֵי שְׁלֹמֹה belongs to verse 1. The saying is antithetic: בֵּן חָכָם יְשַׂמַּח אָב against וּבֵן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ. The second line has no verb, and the conjunction ו before בֵּן means 'but'. The pairs are 'wise son' and 'foolish son', and 'father' and 'mother', so the saying is about what a child's conduct does to the parents.

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: A wise son gathereth in summer; but a son that doeth shamefully sleepeth in harvest.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Both lines are nominal clauses with a participial subject. אֹגֵר בַּקַּיִץ, 'the one who gathers in summer', is בֵּן מַשְׂכִּיל, 'a wise son'. נִרְדָּם בַּקָּצִיר, 'the one who sleeps in harvest', is בֵּן מֵבִישׁ, 'a son who brings shame'. The summer and the harvest are the same season, and the saying is about doing the work at the right time.

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: He that walketh uprightly walketh securely; but he that perverteth his ways shall be found out.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A participle as subject and a yiqtol as predicate. הוֹלֵךְ בַּתֹּם יֵלֶךְ בֶּטַח is 'the one who walks in integrity walks in security'. The second line, וּמְעַקֵּשׁ דְּרָכָיו יִוָּדֵעַ, is 'but the one who twists his ways will be found out', with another participle as subject. The sense of the yiqtol is general: what regularly happens.

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The rare noun סְגוֹר stands in the first line, and כֶּסֶף, 'silver', in the second. Both are things given in exchange or weighed out as a price: מְחִירָהּ. The parallel suggests that סְגוֹר is something precious, but it does not fix the exact meaning.

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: Who determined the measures thereof, if thou knowest? Or who stretched the line upon it?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The noun מְמַדֶּיהָ occurs only here in the analysed text. The question is 'who set its (the earth's) measurements?', and the second line has נָטָה עָלֶיהָ קָו, 'who stretched a line over it?'. The measuring line makes 'measurements' a good guess, and no other use of the word can check it.

practice.prompt: The second line of this verse, וּבֵן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ, has no verb. How is it read?

options: As a clause with the verb יְשַׂמַּח carried over
As a nominal clause: 'a foolish son (is) the grief of his mother'
practice.explain: The line has a subject, בֵּן כְּסִיל, and a predicate, תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ. It is a nominal clause. The verb of the first line is about gladdening and does not fit the second line.

practice.prompt: What is the phrase אֹגֵר בַּקַּיִץ in this verse?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: A wise son gathereth in summer; but a son that doeth shamefully sleepeth in harvest.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A participial subject: 'the one who gathers in summer', who is a wise son
practice.explain: אֹגֵר is a Qal participle, and it is the subject of a nominal clause whose predicate is בֵּן מַשְׂכִּיל. The saying names the person by what he does.

practice.prompt: In the second line the word שֵׁם answers a word of the first line. Which?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing; but the name of the wicked shall rot.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: זֵכֶר, 'memory', is the word that answers שֵׁם, 'name'. The righteous man's memory is for blessing, and the wicked man's name will rot. The other pairs are צַדִּיק // רְשָׁעִים and לִבְרָכָה // יִרְקָב.

practice.prompt: The question וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא recurs in a nearly identical form in 28:20. What does a repeated line like this do?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: But wisdom, where shall it be found? And where is the place of understanding?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It shows that the text is damaged
It marks a refrain that returns to the poem's main question: where is wisdom found?
It is a command to the reader
practice.explain: The question is the centre of the poem. Its return in 28:20 divides the poem into parts, and the answer comes after it.

practice.prompt: In the second line, which phrase answers כּוֹכְבֵי בֹקֶר, 'morning stars'?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: The two lines make a pair of subjects: the morning stars and all the sons of God. They sing and shout together. The parallel suggests that the poet means the same company by two names, but it is a guide, not a proof.

practice.explain: עָרַ֣בְתָּ is Qal, qatal (perfect), perfect, 2nd person, masculine, singular, from עָרַב (take on pledge, give in pledge).

check.prompt: What is הוֹלֵךְ בַּתֹּם at the start of the verse, and how does it function?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: He that walketh uprightly walketh securely; but he that perverteth his ways shall be found out.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A participle used as the subject: 'the one who walks in integrity'
check.explain: הוֹלֵךְ is a Qal participle of הָלַךְ. It names the person, and the predicate is the yiqtol יֵלֶךְ בֶּטַח, 'walks in security'. The same participle-then-verb pattern is common in sayings.

check.prompt: Which verb in the second line is the counterpart of תְּעוֹרֵר, 'stirs up'?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: Hatred stirs up (תְּעוֹרֵר) strife, and love covers (תְּכַסֶּה) wrongs. The two subjects, שִׂנְאָה and אַהֲבָה, are opposites, and the two verbs are opposite actions. אַהֲבָה is the subject, not the verb.

check.prompt: What figure is מְקוֹר חַיִּים פִּי צַדִּיק, 'the mouth of the righteous is a spring of life'?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life; but the mouth of the wicked concealeth violence.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A metaphor in a nominal clause: the mouth is a spring
check.explain: There is no 'like' and no verb. The clause says that the righteous man's mouth is a spring of life. The second line, with the identical words of 10:6, sets the wicked man's mouth beside it.

check.prompt: What does the ו of וּצְדָקָה at the start of the second line do?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing; but righteousness delivereth from death.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It makes a contrast with the first line: 'but righteousness delivers from death'
It joins the line to the first as 'and also'
It turns the line into a question
check.explain: In an antithetic saying the ו at the start of the second line is read as 'but'. The first line says that treasures of wickedness do not profit, the second that righteousness rescues.

check.prompt: The noun סְגוֹר is rare. What does its parallel in the second line suggest about it?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a precious thing given in exchange, ranked with silver; this is a guide and not a proof
It is a verb meaning 'to close'
check.explain: The second line has כֶּסֶף weighed out as a price. So סְגוֹר stands in a line about what could be given in exchange. The parallel gives the kind of thing, not an exact gloss, and the word has a different use in Hosea 13:8.

check.prompt: The noun מְמַדֶּיהָ occurs only here in the analysed text. What in the second line helps with its sense?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: Who determined the measures thereof, if thou knowest? Or who stretched the line upon it?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The word קָו, 'line', in the question about stretching a line over the earth
check.explain: A measuring line suggests that the first line is about measurements: 'who set its measurements?'. The guess comes from the partner line, and since no other use exists to check it, it remains a guess.

check.prompt: What does תְּהוֹם אָמַר לֹא בִי הִיא mean, and what is הִיא?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: The deep saith: 'It is not in me'; and the sea saith: 'It is not with me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'The deep says: she is the sea'; הִיא is a place
'The deep says: it is not in me'; הִיא is wisdom, a feminine word, the subject of a clause with no verb
check.explain: The clause has a negative, a preposition with the suffix 'me', and a pronoun הִיא. The pronoun is feminine because it stands for wisdom, חָכְמָה, the subject of the poem. The next line says the same of the sea.

check.prompt: What is בְּיָסְדִי אָרֶץ in 'where were you when I ... the earth'?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? Declare, if thou hast the understanding.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A time clause: ב with an infinitive construct and the suffix 'I' as its subject, 'when I founded the earth'
A noun in the construct state before אָרֶץ
check.explain: בְּיָסְדִי is the preposition ב, the infinitive construct of יָסַד, and the ending 'my'. The suffix on an infinitive can be the subject of the action: 'in my founding the earth'. אָרֶץ is its object.

check.prompt: What is חֲכַם לֵב in the first line?

quoted.title: Proverbs
quoted.english: The wise in heart will receive commandments; but a prating fool shall fall.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: An adjective in the construct state before a noun: 'the wise of heart'
check.explain: חֲכַם is the construct form of the adjective חָכָם, and לֵב completes it: 'wise of heart'. It is the subject of יִקַּח, and the second line has the matching אֱוִיל שְׂפָתַיִם, 'foolish of lips'.

reading.why: Twelve antithetic sayings that show the whole toolkit: the heading in verse 1, verbless lines (10:1), participles as subjects (10:5, 10:9), pairs of opposites (10:7, 10:12), and one line repeated between verses (10:6 and 10:11). Read each verse by finding its two lines and what answers what.
